When frazjp65 recaptured with 5...Nxd5?, unleashing a discovered attack on your knight, they walked straight into theoretical trouble. You didn't hesitate and struck with the classic Fried Liver sacrifice 6.Nxf7!, executing a fork on Black's queen and rook that dragged their king out into the open.

After 7.Qf3+, Black panicked and retreated with 7...Ke8? instead of stepping up to e6. You punished this immediately with 8.Bxd5!. Black then collapsed completely by playing 8...Qxd5?, which walked into a clean queen capture with 9.Qxd5!. Black gave up another bishop on the very next turn with 10.Qxe6+, leaving you up massive material.

With the queen and material firmly in hand, you converted cleanly without a single inaccuracy. You castled safely, traded down when convenient with 19.Qd3 Bxa3 20.Qxa3, and used your rooks to break open the center. By the time you landed 31.Qd7+, Black had no escape.

review.turning_point: The game was decided right out of the opening when Black walked into 6.Nxf7! and then blundered their queen on move 8 with 8...Qxd5?.
review.focus: Keep this sharp theoretical readiness in your opening repertoire; executing moves like 6.Nxf7! instantly converts opponent mistakes into decisive advantages.

Fortunately, White missed the strongest replies and later traded rooks with 33.Rxe7??. You recaptured cleanly with 33...Kxe7! to enter an advantageous king-and-pawn endgame.

Instead of fixing White's weaknesses with 38...c4, you played 38...e4??, locking down the position and creating fatal weaknesses. Even then, both sides traded inaccuracies until 41...cxb4+?? gave White an active outside passed pawn that decided the game.

review.focus: In pure king-and-pawn endgames, calculate king opposition and pawn breaks before advancing; on 48...Ke5??, playing 48...Kc5 would have kept the opposition and held the draw.

After White swapped on f6, you had a sharp opportunity to target the knight on f3. The engine preferred 11...Bxf3 taking advantage of the pin against the d1-queen, but you pushed 11...g5 instead. That gave White the tempo needed to plant a strong knight on d5 with 12.Nd5, forcing your bishop back to g7.

White stepped up the pressure with 14.Qa4, and instead of tucking your king away safely with 14...O-O, you pushed forward with 14...g4. While this left your position overextended and vulnerable, White ran out of time on move 14, handing you the win.

review.focus: Prioritize king safety before launching flank attacks—moves like 14...O-O would have secured your position instead of overextending with 14...g4.

sections.text: Black immediately lashed out with 10...Nxe4, executing a discovered attack on your bishop at h4 while challenging your queen. Rather than capturing their knight with 11.Nxe4 d5 12.Nxc6 bxc6 13.Bxe7 Qxe7, which would have won material for you, you played 11.Bxe7. That allowed 11...Nxd2, picking off your queen.

After 12.Bxd8, Black erred in return with 12...Nxf1 instead of taking back with their king. You had a chance to stay level with 13.Nxc6, but 13.Bh4 retreated the bishop and left your opponent up a full piece after 13...Nd2 14.Bd3, prompting an early resignation.

review.turning_point: The game hinged on 11.Bxe7, where missing 11.Nxe4 allowed Black to capture your queen with 11...Nxd2 and seize control.
review.focus: When your opponent triggers a tactical skirmish like 10...Nxe4, take a deep breath to calculate direct captures on the offending piece before making counter-attacks.

sections.text: You chose the Albin Countergambit and quickly generated central activity. After simplifying with 8...Bxf3 and 9...Nxe5, you reached a comfortable position. White slipped with 10.Qd5, setting up a skewer against d8 and your bishop, but trading queens and castling queenside kept your initiative alive.

Your central pressure paid off when you punished 16.h3 with 16...Nxe4!, winning a pawn. After 18.Rf1, your jump 18...Nf4! targeted the pinned bishop on e2 and expanded your advantage to +4.5 as you cleaned up with 19...Rxd5.

You gave back much of your edge with 21...Re7, setting up a pin on e2 instead of keeping your active knight with 21...Nf4. Then on move 29, White blundered with 29.Bf5, but you missed the free piece with 29...Nxf5 and played 29...b6 instead, sliding into an equal knight-versus-bishop ending.

You defended resiliently for many moves, but under time pressure, the position cracked. 47...Ne7 allowed the white king inside, and 48...Ng8 trapped your own knight, allowing 49.Kxg8 where the piece was lost and the game decided.

review.turning_point: After defending a level endgame, 47...Ne7 and 48...Ng8 trapped your knight, handing White a decisive material advantage.
review.focus: Stay alert for loose pieces even deep into the endgame; 29...b6 missed capturing the hanging bishop with 29...Nxf5.

sections.text: Against your higher-rated opponent's Sicilian Löwenthal, you developed smoothly through the opening until move 10. You opted for 10.Nd5, but leaving the e4-pawn undefended allowed 10...Nxe4, handing Black an extra center pawn and active pieces.

Seeking counterplay, you pushed 16.g4, but Black struck back on the queenside with 16...b5. After 17.cxb5 axb5 18.Bxb5?! Bxd5, Black collected your knight on d5 and maintained firm control over the center.

Black steadily advanced their central pawns and invaded with 25...Qxb2. On move 26, Black slipped with 26...Nd2, delivering a fork against your rooks on f1 and f3. You responded with 27.R1f2 to set up a pin on the d2-knight along the second rank, but 27...Nxf3+ simplified into a winning rook-up endgame for Black before your clock ran out.

review.turning_point: 10.Nd5 dropped the central e4-pawn without compensation, giving Black an early initiative they never surrendered.
review.focus: Keep a close eye on central pawn tension and undefended pawns before leaping forward with knight maneuvers like 10.Nd5.

sections.text: The game started out in a Symmetrical English, but your 6...e5 proved to be an early blunder that allowed White to strike with 7.Nxe5. You stayed alert and looked for tactical chances. After 16...Re6, White walked into disaster with 17.Bxe6. You punished the mistake instantly with 17...Nf3+!, an intermezzo that delivered check and unleashed a discovered attack by your bishop on d6 against White's bishop on f4. After 18.Kg2 Nxd2, you captured White's queen and took complete control.

Ahead massive material, you converted smoothly. You traded rooks with 26...Rxe2 27.Kxe2, centralized your queen, and infiltrated with 33...Qe2. White's remaining pawns quickly fell, and after 36...Qxb3, White resigned.

review.turning_point: White's 17.Bxe6 overlooked your tactical shot 17...Nf3+!, which won White's queen on d2 and decided the contest on the spot.
review.focus: Take extra care with diagonal alignments on your fianchettoed bishop; 6...e5 dropped a central pawn to 7.Nxe5 due to the pressure on b7.

White then blundered with 12.Bxe7??, offering you a massive tactical shot. Instead of recapturing immediately, taking the knight with 12...exf3 would have won material while unmasking a threat on White's queen. After 12...Qxe7??, White jumped in with 13.Nxd5. Stepping into 13...Qe6?? allowed 14.Nxc7+, and with your queen and king caught, the game was over.

review.turning_point: The decisive swing came on move 12: after White's 12.Bxe7??, finding the intermediate capture 12...exf3 would have won a piece, but 12...Qxe7?? allowed White to regain control with 13.Nxd5.
review.focus: Look for intermediate captures (in-between moves) before making automatic recaptures, as missed with 12...Qxe7.

review.turning_point: The endgame remained fully playable until 44.Kg1?? stepped into the fatal 44...Nf3+ fork, losing the rook on e1.
review.focus: Maintain king safety in low-time endgames: avoid walking into simple knight forks like 44.Kg1 instead of 44.Kg3.

review.focus: In time trouble, watch out for double attacks like 38.Qc8+, where intervening with 38...Rd8 would have maintained the defense of your bishop on a8.

White was playing for rapid piece development, while your goal was to untangle and secure your king.

White castled, and you developed with 6...Be7 before pushing 7...d5 to challenge White's light-squared bishop in the center. When White took on f6 with 8.Bxf6, you chose 8...gxf6?! instead of recapturing with your bishop. While it kept a pawn on d5, it damaged your kingside structure and left White active.

After White captured back on d5 with 9.Bxd5, the position required precise handling. Kicking the bishop with 9...c6 was necessary to force 10.Bb3 and keep your position solid. Instead, 9...Be6?? left your position critically compromised, prompting an immediate resignation.

review.turning_point: The game came to an abrupt end on 9...Be6??, which collapsed your defense right after the opening complications.
review.focus: Take an extra moment to calculate direct responses to central threats instead of offering quick piece trades, as seen on 9...Be6.

With the dark squares around White's king stripped bare, you methodically tightened the noose. You anchored your knight on d3 and mobilized your kingside pawns with 20...f5 and 22...f4. After White took on f4, you uncorked 23...Nxf4+!, breaking open the defensive shell.

White tried desperately to hold on, but your rooks joined the party to finish the job. After lifting your rook with 28...Re6 and checking along the h-file with 30...Rh6+, you brought your final piece into the attack with 32...Rf8. White gave up the exchange with 33.Rxd3, but it only delayed the inevitable before 34...Qe2# delivered checkmate.

review.turning_point: White's blunder 12.c4 handed you the piece on h3, leaving their king fatally exposed on the dark squares for the rest of the game.
review.focus: Look for direct attacking follow-ups instead of routine recaptures: on move 17, 17...Ng4 would have forced immediate mate threats rather than 17...Nxd5.

Instead of securing your king and completing development, you went hunting for extra material while your king remained stuck in the center. When Black challenged the queen with 18...Bc8, grabbing yet another pawn with 19.Qxc6 walk right into disaster along the open e-file.

You used your extra material to activate both rooks on the seventh rank, sweeping up pawns on c2 and c4. Although the position became chaotic as White tried to generate threats against your king, you found 38...Rh1+!, a crushing skewer along the back rank against White's king and rook.

Up a full rook in the endgame, time trouble crept in and you blundered your rook with 44...Rd6??, allowing 45.Bxd6. Fortunately, your passed c-pawn was unstoppable. White failed to stop the runner, and you sealed the win with 48...c1=Q+! on the back rank just before White flagged.

review.turning_point: White's blunder 19.Nxf5?? handed you a free knight with 19...Nxf5!, giving you a decisive material advantage that you carried into the endgame.
review.focus: In winning endgames with low time, keep your heavy pieces safe from simple bishop captures instead of giving them away as happened on 44...Rd6??.

review.turning_point: Black's 20...Qxb2 overlooked the unstoppable mate, allowing you to finish the game immediately with 21.Qxa7+ and 22.Nd6#.
review.focus: King safety during tactical rushes; on move 19.Nb5, launching an attack while your own king is exposed can backfire against precise defense.

review.turning_point: The game tipped decisively when you played 10...Qg6, overlooking that your knight on d4 was unprotected and allowing 11.cxd4.
review.focus: Keep track of your loose pieces before continuing an attack, as 10...Qg6 left the d4-knight completely hanging.

review.focus: Always verify which of your pieces are undefended when moving your queen, as 24...Qb5 left your bishop on e4 unprotected and nearly cost you the game.

review.focus: Keep your pieces safely defended in the endgame to prevent sudden material drops like 55.Ke3.
